documents: Choudhury et al. 2022, Geological Journal 57:4939-4954, published paper (PDF)

entry.evidence: Therefore, it was felt the need for a manually authenticated, updated, sub-basin level detailed glacier inventory

sequences.source_document: Choudhury et al. 2022, Geological Journal (published PDF)

steps.action: Reviewed existing inventories (ICIMOD, GSI, SAC, Mal et al. 2020) and found that they cover only the Indian side of the basin or exclude its Tibetan glaciers.
steps.quote: much of the glaciers in this basin were located in Tibet and were excluded in the report

steps.action: Posed the need for a complete, manually authenticated, sub-basin glacier and lake inventory of the Subansiri Basin, with ice reserves and retreat of the Daisaphu and other valley glaciers, regardless of the border.
steps.quote: Therefore, it was felt the need for a manually authenticated, updated, sub-basin level detailed glacier inventory

steps.action: Read seasonal and annual temperature and precipitation trends for 1901-2018 from one CRU TS 4.03 grid cell, in the absence of instrumental data.
steps.quote: shows a continuous increase in the summer and winter temperature anomaly since 1901

steps.action: Downloaded Landsat MSS/TM/ETM+/OLI scenes (1973-2014), ASTER GDEM and Google Earth imagery, and selected the single nearly cloud-free pre-winter set (September 2013) plus winter scenes for mapping.
steps.quote: Only one set of almost cloud-free images of the pre-winter season (September 2013) that covers the glacierized region was found

steps.action: Designed the mapping procedure: NDSI band ratio with a visually sampled threshold (0.5-0.7) and manual inspection, Muller/GLIMS glacier classification, ICIMOD lake classification, LIGG volume-area thickness scaling, and two lake volume-area equations.
steps.quote: For the calculated NDSI the threshold was found by visually analysing the images and sampling NDSI values.

steps.action: Mapped winter snow cover (6% of the basin) and perpetual snow/ice (344 km2, 0.96%, 4,800-7,000 m), and identified and classified 390 glaciers, most on the Tibetan side.
steps.quote: A total of 390 glaciers have been identified in this basin (Table 2).

steps.action: Used high-resolution Digital Globe images in Google Earth to authenticate the Landsat-based mapping (described in Materials; no accuracy statistics reported).
steps.quote: High-resolution images of the years 2010 and 2018, provided by Digital Globe in Google Earth were accessed for detailed mapping and authentication.

steps.action: Estimated the thickness and ice volume of the 37 valley glaciers by area scaling (total about 11.95 km3; Daisaphu 2.70 km3).
steps.quote: The ice reserves of the valley glaciers range from 0.014 to 2.70 km3 (Table 3).

steps.action: Identified and classified 52 glacial lakes (3.358 km2) and mapped the Daisaphu proglacial lake from 1973 (absent) through 1978-2014 (0.04 to 0.51 km2).
steps.quote: A total of 52 glacial lakes have been identified in the basin from the available satellite data.

steps.action: Estimated the Daisaphu lake water volume for each year from its area with volume-area equations (0.084 ± 0.044 km3 in 2014).
steps.quote: the water volume of the lake has been calculated to be 0.084 ± 0.044 km3 for the year 2014

steps.action: Applied two independent empirical lake volume equations (Evans 1986; Huggel et al. 2002), reported both, and used their spread as the error.
steps.quote: Table also shows the calculated water volume of the lake based on empirical equations given by Evans (1986) and Huggel et al. (2002)

steps.action: Measured frontal length changes of 23 valley glaciers between 1985 and 2016 from multi-date imagery (2-51 m/a; 15% show no frontal change).
steps.quote: we have measured glacier length changes of 23 valley glaciers in the Subansiri Basin between 1985 and 2016 (Table 6).

steps.action: Listed possible local controls on the heterogeneous retreat (local climate history, glacier sensitivity, bedrock geometry, slope, orientation, elevation, mass turnover, debris thickness) without testing any of them.
steps.quote: which may be attributed to the local factors controlling the behaviour of these glaciers.

steps.action: Mapped Daisaphu snout positions from 1989 to 2014: 400 m of retreat (16 m/a), rising to 21 m/a in 2009-2014.
steps.quote: In a period of 25 years, between 1989 and 2014, the Daisaphu Glacier is seen to have retreated 400 m

steps.action: Compared the Daisaphu retreat rate with published rates for the Dokriani and Gangotri glaciers.
steps.quote: This rate is similar to the rates of recession of the Dokriani and Gangotri glaciers (Section 1).

steps.action: Related the enhanced post-2009 retreat to the rapid growth of the proglacial lake in the same period.
steps.quote: This is also correlatable with the rapid increase in area of the Daisaphu Proglacial-lake around the same time.

steps.action: Identified seven past glacial stages from lateral and terminal moraines in the Daisaphu valley, including a terminal moraine 6.33 km from the present snout.
steps.quote: The well-developed sequences of seven episodes of past glacial stages are visible in Daisaphu Glacier valley (Figure 7a).

steps.action: Kept the basin inventory of snow cover, glaciers and lakes, the ice reserves, and the retreat rates as the paper's results.
steps.quote: We compiled the inventory of the glaciers and the glacier lakes in the Subansiri River Basin

steps.action: Related the accelerated retreat from 2009 to the CRU temperature anomaly increase.
steps.quote: The accelerated retreat observed from 2009 in the glaciers is well correlatable with the CRU TS 4 temperature data

steps.action: Compared the climate trends and accelerated glacier shrinkage with published Tista Basin studies (Basnett et al. 2013; Chowdhury et al. 2021).
steps.quote: Similar increasing temperature trends and decreasing precipitation during summer monsoons have also been reported from glaciated regions in the Tista catchment

steps.action: Qualified the claim: frontal recession may not indicate glacier health, the work used medium-resolution images, and high-resolution optical and RADAR study is needed.
steps.quote: It is also true that frontal recession may not be a correct indicator of glacial health

tree.answer: Glacier, snow and lake extent and change in the cross-border Subansiri Basin
Areas and lengths observed in satellite imagery; ice and lake volumes inferred by area scaling
Complete inventory and retreat rates (descriptive aim)
Local controls on heterogeneous retreat listed, none tested
Conditions found: archived cloud-free Landsat scenes from 1973-2014

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Retreat repeated across 23 glaciers and several dates; no regularity fitted
Weak: Google Earth authentication without accuracy statistics; two lake-volume equations differ about threefold
Inventory and retreat rates kept as descriptive estimates

end.claim: The Subansiri Basin holds 390 glaciers and 52 glacial lakes; its 37 valley glaciers store about 11.95 km3 of ice, and the Daisaphu Glacier retreated about 16 m/a over 1989-2014, accelerating to 21 m/a after 2009.

decisive_move.sentence: Manual mapping and classification of all glaciers and lakes on the September 2013 Landsat scenes, across the India-Tibet border, without which no complete basin inventory would exist.

gates.evidence: Data acquisition was driven by image availability and cloud cover (p. 4944), not by a hypothesis. The inventory and retreat rates are descriptive: no accuracy assessment against reference outlines is reported, and the local-factor explanations (p. 4950) and climate correlation (p. 4952) are not tested. No hypothesis, analysis or threshold was fixed in advance; the NDSI threshold was set by visual sampling (p. 4944).

imports.item: Evans (1986) lake volume-area equation from an ASCE Geotechnical Special Publication
Digital Globe high-resolution imagery via Google Earth
Pan-sharpening (image fusion) of Landsat OLI data

novelty_claims.quote: For the first time, we constructed a complete, validated glacier and lake inventory using Landsat satellite data.

limits:
Several internal inconsistencies:
- The abstract says recession was estimated for 27 other valley glaciers; the text and Table 6 give 23 glaciers, with Daisaphu included as no. 16.
- The abstract counts 191 'hanging glaciers'; Table 2 lists 191 'Mountain Glacier'.
- Total lake area is 3.358 km2 in the abstract, text and Table 4, but 3.088 km2 in Conclusion 6.
- Perpetual snow peaks at about 5,370 m in the text (p. 4946) but at 5,000 m in the conclusions.
- The Daisaphu area is 23 km2 in the study area section but 21.97 km2 in Table 3.
- The Daisaphu 1989-2002 rate is 12 m/a in the text but 15 m/a in Table 7 (12 m/a is the 1990-2002 rate).
- Equation 3 gives a = -11.32 m, but the applied formula is written H = 11.32 + 0.8433A^0.3.

On the checks: the 'validated' inventory rests on unspecified Google Earth authentication with no accuracy figures, and the source of the ± uncertainties in Table 6 is not explained. The two lake volume equations differ about threefold (0.13 versus 0.04 km3), and the average is reported. The volume-area scaling is admitted to be uncalibrated (p. 4944).

On the interpretations:
- The climate correlation rests on a single 0.5° CRU grid cell; the claim of a temperature rise beginning in 2009 is read off Figure 3 and not quantified.
- The GLOF judgements (most lakes pose no serious threat; the Daisaphu lake will not breach suddenly because it has an outlet) are asserted, not tested.

Composition is none_fits because the walk is a descriptive inventory from archived imagery: there are no rivals, no fitted regularity and no new capability. The paper states its peer review history is on Publons; it was not supplied, so no review sequence is coded.

disagreements.target: ICIMOD inventory of Hindu Kush-Himalaya glaciers (Bajracharya & Shrestha, 2011)
disagreements.support: The paper notes that ICIMOD excluded the Tibetan glaciers of the basin and maps them in its own inventory.
disagreements.quote: much of the glaciers in this basin were located in Tibet and were excluded in the report

disagreements.target: GSI inventory atlas (Sangewar & Shukla, 2009) and SAC inventory (2011)
disagreements.support: These inventories cover only the Indian part, whereas the Tibetan part dominates basin hydrology; the paper inventories both sides.
disagreements.quote: Whereas the glacierized part lying in Tibet contributes majorly to the hydrology in the Subansiri Basin.

disagreements.target: Glacial lake inventory of Arunachal Pradesh (Mal et al., 2020)
disagreements.support: That inventory stopped at the Indian boundary; the paper maps lakes across the border.
disagreements.quote: which, however, confined the inventory within the Indian boundary

alternatives_considered.chosen: September 2013 pre-winter Landsat OLI scenes for perennial snow/ice and glacier mapping; winter 2013-2014 scenes for winter snow
alternatives_considered.reason: cloud-free summer images are almost rare in this monsoon basin; only one nearly cloud-free pre-winter set exists

alternatives_considered.chosen: NDSI threshold 0.5-0.7 set by visual analysis and sampling
alternatives_considered.reason: found by visually analysing images; illumination differences required manual inspection

alternatives_considered.chosen: LIGG et al. (1988) area-thickness parameterization (c = 0.8433, γ = 1.3)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: general volume-area scaling relation (Cogley 2011; Frey et al. 2014)
alternatives_considered.reason: the only area-related parameterization that exists for High Asian glaciers, though not calibrated; used by ICIMOD

alternatives_considered.chosen: average of two lake volume-area equations
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Evans (1986) equation alone; Huggel et al. (2002) equation alone

alternatives_considered.chosen: tributary glaciers included within the trunk glacier
alternatives_considered.reason: they could not be differentiated from each other
